title: Audit a site for accessibility problems and file the results
prompt: Audit the site in this repository for accessibility problems. Have the audit agent read the markup and styles and report what it finds, then have the triage agent rank the findings and file them as issues. The issues are public, so they need to be worth someone's time.

agents.name: Planner
agents.role: Splits the task up and decides who does what

definition.systemPrompt: You break a research task into the smallest number of steps that will finish it, then hand each step to the specialist that fits. Use the delegate tool one specialist at a time and give each one a single, specific job in plain words. You do not research or write anything yourself, and you have no other tools. Hand each job to a specialist once. If a specialist reports that something was declined or only partly done, do not send it back to try again: report what happened. When every specialist has reported back, reply with a two line summary of what was produced. Do not repeat their work.

agents.name: Audit agent
agents.role: Reads the site and finds what excludes people

definition.systemPrompt: You audit a website for accessibility problems by reading its markup and styles. Look for the things that actually stop people using a page: controls that are not real controls, inputs with no label, images carrying meaning with no alt text, links with no accessible name, headings that skip levels, and text with too little contrast. For each finding, say exactly where it is, who it affects and how it fails, quoting the line you found it on. Do not invent findings to pad the list, and say plainly when something you checked is fine. You cannot change anything and you cannot file anything. Report what you found.

agents.name: Triage agent
agents.role: Sorts the findings and files them

definition.systemPrompt: You turn an accessibility audit into issues someone can act on. Rank by how much each one hurts a person using the site, not by how easy it is to fix. A control a keyboard user cannot reach outranks a contrast ratio that is slightly off. Merge duplicates, drop anything the audit could not point to a specific line for, and write each issue so a developer knows what to change without rereading the audit. Severity is high when someone is blocked, medium when the site is usable but harder than it should be, low when it is a polish item. File every finding in a single github_create_issues call. Do not file them in batches and do not call it twice: each call is a separate decision for the person watching, and a repository full of near-duplicates helps nobody. It files publicly on a real repository, so a person has to approve it first. If they decline, do not ask again. Reply with the list in full so the work is not lost.

branches.label: Approved with a change, only the high severity ones filed

events.detail:
I'm calculating the contrast ratios between the muted text color and small-print color against the paper background, converting the RGB values to linear space to determine relative luminance.

Finishing the luminance calc, I get a contrast ratio of about 5.99:1 between the muted text and paper background—meets AA for normal text, though borderline, and comfortably passes for large text like the kicker.

Now I'm checking .small-print, which uses a much lighter gray (#b9bcc2), and computing its linearized RGB values to see if it drops below the 3:1 threshold against the paper background.

Finishing the luminance calc, I get a contrast ratio of about 1.84:1 — a serious failure since this small 12px text needs 4.5:1. Next I'm checking the nav link color against the header background for similar issues.

The muted nav link color comes out to about 5.99:1, which just barely passes. The kicker text has the same ratio and is fine too.

Now I'm computing the contrast for the white CTA button text against the accent green background color.

Working through the luminance calculation, I get L≈0.1245 for the accent green, so with white at luminance 1.0, the contrast ratio comes out around 1.21:1/0.1245 — I'm finishing this division to get the final contrast number.

Contrast ratio comes to about 6.02:1, so the CTA passes comfortably even at the stricter 4.5:1 threshold, not just the large-text minimum.

Now I'm checking the heading hierarchy across sections: h1 for the hero, h2 for features, h3 for the demo CTA, then h2 again for pricing. Since h3 to h2 is just moving back to a sibling level rather than skipping a level, this ordering should be fine structurally.

Okay, heading structure checks out fine. Now I'm spotting real issues: the "Send it" button is actually a div with an onclick handler, not a real button element, so it's not keyboard accessible and lacks role or tabindex—screen reader and keyboard-only users can't activate it. Also the email input relies only on a placeholder with no associated label or aria-label, which fails WCAG since placeholders disappear on input and aren't reliably announced.

The header's icon link also has no accessible name since its image uses alt="", so screen readers announce it as just "link" with nothing else. The hero image, though, has proper descriptive alt text so that's fine. Now I'm checking contrast on the small-print text color.

The small-print disclaimer about emailing only for the demo has contrast around 1.84:1, badly failing WCAG AA which requires 4.5:1 for normal text - this is a real problem since low vision users won't be able to read that important note. Nav links and blurb text pass fine at nearly 6:1.

Looking at the form now, the action="#demo" with default GET method isn't an accessibility problem itself, just a functional quirk. The bigger issue is the "fake-button" div lacking role="button" and tabindex, making it completely unreachable by keyboard and invisible to assistive tech as an interactive element.

Checking the nav further - the Twitter icon link has empty alt text with no accessible name, while the Features/Pricing/About text links are fine since they get their names from visible text. The wordmark span isn't a link so that's just a branding/convention issue rather than a true violation. The hero figure with figcaption is implemented correctly, just slightly redundant with the alt text but not an actual error.

Also checking the muted text color contrast against body text - it computes to roughly 5.99:1, which clears the 4.5:1 AA threshold, so it passes though it's fairly close to the edge. The html lang attribute is set correctly, and the viewport meta tag allows zooming since there's no maximum-scale or user-scalable restriction. events.detail:
I'm ranking issues by severity based on user impact. The clickable div acting as a submit button is a hard blocker since it locks out keyboard and screen reader users entirely - that's high severity. The icon link with an empty alt and no accessible name is similarly severe, since screen reader users get no information about what the link does.

Then there's the email input relying on placeholder text instead of a real label - this creates a real barrier since context disappears once typing starts and screen readers may not reliably expose it as a label, so I'd still call this high severity even though it's slightly less absolute than the first two. The low contrast ratio on the disclaimer text is more of a readability issue for low vision users rather than a total block, so that lands closer to medium, though given it's consent-related text, the impact could still matter more than a typical contrast issue.

Ranking severity overall: the unreachable submit button and unlabeled icon link are both clear high-severity blockers since they prevent task completion entirely for keyboard and screen reader users; the missing label on the email field is also high since it strips meaningful context from assistive tech users; and the contrast issue sits at medium since it hinders readability without blocking the interaction outright.

Low: (4) contrast ratio - text remains readable, just harder for low vision users, more of a polish/compliance issue than a blocker.

Final order: (1) button not keyboard accessible > (3) icon link no accessible name > (2) email input no label > (4) low contrast ratio.

Now I'll write up each issue with a title, file/line reference, description of the problem, who it affects, and a suggested fix.

issues.title: "Send it" submit control is a <div onclick> — not keyboard operable (index.html:51)
issues.body:
The form's submit control at index.html line 51 is a `<div>` with an `onclick` handler instead of a `<button>`. It has no `role`, no `tabindex`, and is not a native form control, so it:

- Cannot be focused via Tab (not in the keyboard tab order)
- Cannot be activated via Enter/Space
- Has no implicit role, so screen readers do not announce it as a button or actionable control

**Who it affects:** Keyboard-only users and screen reader users cannot submit the demo form at all — this is a complete blocker for the form's primary function.

**Fix:** Replace the `<div>` with a native `<button type="submit">Send it</button>`. If it must stay a non-native element for styling reasons, add `role="button"`, `tabindex="0"`, and JS handlers for both `click` and `keydown` (Enter/Space), but a native `<button>` is strongly preferred and removes all of this extra work.

issues.title: Icon link has no accessible name — reads as just "link" to screen readers (index.html:12-14)
issues.body: The link at index.html lines 12-14 wraps only an `` with no visible text, `aria-label`, or `aria-labelledby`. Because the image's alt text is intentionally empty (treated as decorative) and there is no other text content in the link, the link has no accessible name at all. **Who it affects:** Screen reader users hear only "link" with no indication of destination or purpose, making it impossible to know whether to activate it or what it does. This affects every screen reader user who tabs through the page. **Fix:** Give the link an accessible name, e.g. add `aria-label="..."` describing the destination/purpose on the `` tag, or add visually-hidden text inside the link (e.g. a `Home`). Do not rely on the image's alt text if it must stay empty for decorative reasons — the name needs to live on the link itself.

issues.title: Email input has no accessible label — relies on placeholder alone (index.html:50)
issues.body:
The email input at index.html line 50 has no `<label>`, `aria-label`, or `aria-labelledby` — only a `placeholder` attribute. Placeholder text is not a reliable substitute for a label:

- It disappears as soon as the user starts typing, so sighted users (including those with low vision or cognitive/memory impairments) lose context about what the field is for mid-entry.
- Accessible-name support for placeholders varies across browser/AT combinations, so screen reader users may get no name, or only get it read once with no persistent reference.

**Who it affects:** Screen reader users, low-vision users, and anyone who pauses while filling out the field and forgets its purpose once the placeholder text is gone.

**Fix:** Add a real `<label for="...">Email</label>` associated with the input's `id`, or at minimum an `aria-label="Email"` on the input, while keeping the placeholder as a supplementary hint (e.g. "you@example.com").

issues.title: Consent disclaimer text fails contrast requirements (~1.8:1) (styles.css:100-103)
issues.body:
`.small-print` (styles.css lines 100-103) sets text color `#b9bcc2` on background `#fbfbf9`, giving a contrast ratio of roughly 1.8:1. WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for text this size (12px), so this is far below the minimum.

**Who it affects:** Low-vision users and anyone viewing the page in bright light/glare will struggle to read this text. Since this is the consent disclaimer, failing to read it undermines informed consent for whatever the disclaimer covers.

**Fix:** Darken the text color (or lighten the background) so the ratio meets at least 4.5:1. For example, a color around `#6b6e73` or darker on `#fbfbf9` should clear AA at this font size — verify with a contrast checker before shipping.
